sos.note: Police, ambulance and fire anywhere in Puerto Rico. Free from any phone, in English or Spanish.

know_how.title: Money
know_how.text: US dollars. Cards work almost everywhere, but carry cash for taxis (cash only), beach kiosks and market stalls.

know_how.title: Tipping
know_how.text: Like the mainland US: 15 to 20% in restaurants. Check the bill first; larger groups often have a service charge added. Round up for taxis, or about 15%.

know_how.title: Holiday season
know_how.text: Christmas here runs from Thanksgiving to mid-January, with parrandas (carols with drums and güiros), lights and big family meals. Many shops and restaurants close on December 25 and January 1, so book those meals ahead. Three Kings Day is January 6; the celebrations start the evening of January 5.

know_how.title: Holiday food
know_how.text: Lechón (roast pork), pernil and pasteles are the classic Christmas dishes, so pork is everywhere this season. Coquito is a creamy coconut and rum drink. With food notes, ask before ordering.

know_how.title: Beaches and currents
know_how.text: Winter swells can bring strong waves and rip currents to the north coast. Swim at beaches with lifeguards, follow the flags and check the day’s conditions on SwimSafePR (swimsafepr.com), the Tourism Company’s alert service. If caught in a current, swim parallel to the shore or float and raise an arm.

know_how.title: Sun and bugs
know_how.text: The sun is strong even in December: hats, water and shade breaks. Bring insect repellent for evenings and the rainforest, but don’t wear it or lotion in the bio bay.

know_how.title: Critters
know_how.text: Puerto Rico has no dangerous snakes. Mosquitoes are the main nuisance. In the forest, wear closed shoes and don’t lift logs or rocks; large centipedes live there but keep out of sight.

know_how.title: Old San Juan on foot
know_how.text: Steep streets and blue cobblestones that are slippery when wet. Wear shoes with grip, plan downhill routes, and rest in the plazas, which have benches and shade.

know_how.title: Getting home at night
know_how.text: Use Uber or have your hotel or restaurant call a taxi. Don’t walk long, dark stretches between neighborhoods. Check that the car and driver match the app.

know_how.title: Phones and language
know_how.text: US phone plans work as at home: no roaming. Spanish and English are both official languages, and English is widely spoken in tourist areas.

emergency.label: Police, ambulance, fire. English and Spanish.

emergency_note: Pharmacies are easy to find in San Juan, including chains open late or around the clock. Puerto Rico is a US territory, so US citizens need no passport. Other visitors: your country’s consulate in San Juan or embassy in Washington can help with a lost passport.

voice_help.title: iPhone
voice_help.text: Settings, Accessibility, Spoken Content, Voices, Spanish. Pick a voice (Mexico or United States sounds closest) and download its Enhanced or Premium version.

voice_help.title: Android
voice_help.text: Settings, search for Text-to-speech, preferred engine settings, install voice data, Spanish (United States). Menu names vary by phone.

travel_notes: Puerto Rican coffee grows in the central mountains. Order a café con leche.
The domed sentry boxes on the walls are garitas, the island’s best-known symbol.
Old San Juan’s blue cobblestones are adoquines, cast from furnace slag; the story goes they came over as ships’ ballast.
Listen at night for the coquí, a tiny frog that sings its own name.
